removed.pic: One coin, three readings: a long-run frequency plot, a propensity of the setup, and a betting rate; the tool shows where they agree and where they come apart.
A unit square split by hypothesis and evidence with draggable proportions: the posterior is the shaded fraction of the evidence column, computed live.
A test 99% accurate for a disease with 1-in-1000 prevalence: a crowd of 10,000 icons shows that most positives are false, and the prevalence slider changes that.
Enter credences in A and not-A that sum to more than 1: the bookie constructs bets you would accept at those rates and shows a guaranteed loss in every world.
Learn evidence E and zero out the worlds where it fails; renormalising the rest gives the new credence, and a diachronic Dutch book is built against any other update rule.
Pick a hypothesis and an evidence pattern: confirmation is shown as the jump from prior to posterior, and different measures of its size are compared.
Feed in evidence items one by one: log-odds move by the log likelihood ratio of each, and items with a ratio of 1 leave belief untouched however suggestive they seem.
Two agents with very different priors about a coin’s bias watch the same flips: their posteriors merge as data accumulate, with the gap plotted against sample size.
Mercury’s perihelion was known before general relativity: if P(E) = 1 already, conditionalising changes nothing, shown on the probability square collapsing to one column.
In a fair 1000-ticket lottery, believe of each ticket that it will lose (probability 0.999); the conjunction of those beliefs contradicts the certainty that one ticket wins.
An author believes each of 300 claims at 99%: the probability that all are true is computed as about 5%, so the preface’s admission of error is rational.

operations.before: Bayesians model belief as probability and learning as conditionalisation. Dutch-book arguments claim that degrees of belief violating the probability axioms expose one to sure loss, and Bayes’ theorem gives a precise account of when evidence confirms a hypothesis and by how much. The approach explains the base-rate fallacy, but faces problems of its own, including old evidence and the paradoxes of the lottery and the preface.

removed.pic: Condense steam in a closed vessel: the pressure drop sucks water up, limited to about 10 m by the atmosphere; Papin’s cylinder raises a weight with a piston.
Cycle a Newcomen engine: steam fills the cylinder, a cold jet condenses it, and atmospheric pressure drives the piston down to rock the beam and pump; heat wasted reheating the cylinder is tallied.
Replace charcoal with coke in a blast furnace: fuel cost per tonne and the forest area saved are computed, and furnace size can grow.
Bore a cylinder with the cutter supported at both ends: the out-of-roundness falls from a shilling’s thickness to a fraction of it, and steam leakage past the piston drops accordingly.
Toggle between condensing in the cylinder and in a separate cold vessel: the cylinder stays hot, and coal per unit of work falls by roughly two thirds.
Couple the beam to a flywheel through sun-and-planet gearing, then add the centrifugal governor: under changing mill load the speed drifts less with the governor on.
Animate Watt’s linkage: the coupler midpoint traces a nearly straight line through the stroke, with deviation from straightness plotted.
Trace pressure against piston position over a cycle: the enclosed area is the work per stroke, and changing cut-off reshapes the loop.
Raise boiler pressure: engine size per horsepower shrinks enough to move on wheels, while boiler-wall stress rises toward the bursting limit.
Run an ideal engine between a hot and a cold reservoir: its efficiency 1 − T_c/T_h is compared with real engines from Newcomen to modern turbines on one chart.
Stir molten pig iron in a reverberatory furnace to burn off carbon, then pass it through grooved rolls: output per worker is compared with hammering.
Blow air through molten iron: carbon content falls over minutes while the heat of oxidation keeps the bath molten; the price of steel drops on a timeline.
Gear a lathe’s lead screw to the spindle: change gears to cut any pitch, and the thread error is copied from the lead screw onto the work.
Assemble muskets from random parts made to tolerances of different widths: the fraction that fit without filing rises sharply as tolerances tighten.

operations.before: The first steam engines used atmospheric pressure to pump water from mines. Watt’s separate condenser cut their fuel use dramatically, and rotary motion and governors put them to work driving factories. Cheap coke-smelted iron, precision boring and machine tools made bigger and better engines possible, while engineers’ indicator diagrams and Carnot’s analysis began the science of heat engines.
